options: The worker nodes that run Kubernetes pods
The managed Kubernetes control plane that AWS operates on your behalf
An S3 bucket for container images
A single EC2 instance running Docker
questions.explain: aws_eks_cluster provisions the managed Kubernetes API server (the control plane); it does not by itself run any workloads.

questions.q: Why does the `aws_eks_cluster` block reference `role_arn` instead of embedding credentials?
options: EKS clusters cannot use IAM at all
Like the Lambda function in Lesson 27, the cluster assumes an IAM role rather than holding its own long-lived credentials
role_arn is optional and has no real effect
It specifies which subnet the cluster uses
questions.explain: The EKS service assumes the IAM role referenced by role_arn, following the same pattern used for the Lambda function — services assume roles instead of holding static credentials.

questions.q: Why must `vpc_config.subnet_ids` for an EKS cluster include subnets in at least two availability zones?
options: It is only a cosmetic naming convention
EKS requires it for high availability of the control plane
Terraform requires at least two subnets for any resource
It reduces the AWS bill
questions.explain: EKS requires the control plane's network interfaces to span multiple availability zones so the cluster stays available if one zone has an issue.

questions.q: What does the `scaling_config` block on `aws_eks_node_group` control?
options: The Kubernetes version running on the control plane
The desired, minimum, and maximum number of worker nodes in the group
The IAM policy attached to the cluster
The VPC CIDR block
questions.explain: scaling_config sets desired_size, min_size, and max_size, defining how the node group's EC2 instance count can scale with load.

questions.q: How does the AWS EKS pattern in this lesson compare to the AKS pattern from Chapter 5?
options: They share no similarities at all
Both follow the same shape — a managed control plane resource plus a node group or node pool referencing it — differing mainly in resource type prefix and permission model
EKS requires no IAM or access control of any kind
AKS only supports a single node, while EKS supports many
questions.explain: Both clouds follow the same structural pattern: a control plane resource, then a node group/pool resource that references it, wired together with cloud-specific identity (IAM role vs. service principal or managed identity).
